claim: PA splits personal income tax payment plans in two. A 'Standard Plan' is for a plan 'less than 12 months in length' when 'you owe less than $50,000'; it can be set up online in myPATH, by email/fax, or by phone. An 'Extended Plan' is for a plan 'beyond the standard terms', listed as three triggers: 'More than 12 months', 'Balance due is more than $50,000', 'You currently have payment plan with the department'. The page does not say whether one trigger is enough; it lists them as a bulleted set under 'beyond the standard terms'. An extended plan cannot be made in myPATH: 'You must contact the department' by email/fax (RA-RV-CEC-DPP@pa.gov) or phone (717-425-2495 ext. 72972). Before any plan: 'Make sure all previous returns are filed', and balances not yet in collections are added with form REV-638. The myPATH self-service rules (2024 archive) say a plan is not available if 'An active payment plan already exists', or the taxpayer is in wage garnishment, bank attachment or bankruptcy.

extendedPlanTriggers: already on a payment plan with the department
myPATHBlockedIf: wage garnishment or bank attachment in process

uncertainty: The page's wording leaves the edge cases open: a balance of exactly $50,000, or a plan of exactly 12 months, fits neither 'less than' (standard) nor 'more than' (extended). Whether the three extended triggers are alternatives (any one) or cumulative is not stated, though the 'beyond the standard terms' framing implies any one. The custhelp answer on myPATH is a 2024 archive, not read live.
designImplication: Model eligibility for the extended plan as any of: months > 12, balance > 50000, or an existing plan. A player who is already on a plan and adds a new balance gets routed to the extended plan, which is a phone/email negotiation, not a click.

claim: An extended plan request is an email or fax with: full name; Federal EIN, Revenue ID or SSN; mailing address; phone number; 'Number of months you are requesting'; and 'A completed REV-488 Statement of Financial Condition for Individuals'. REV-488 (revision 08-26) has seven sections: I taxpayer and spouse information (names, DOB, SSN, addresses, marital status, W-4 exemptions); II employment for taxpayer and spouse (employer, occupation, paydays, wage earner/partner/sole proprietor); III next of kin or reference, and dependents in the household; IV general financial information (latest PA return filed and its AGI, every bank/credit union/IRA/Keogh/CD account with balance, charge cards and lines of credit with limits and amounts owed, safe deposit boxes and their contents, real estate, life insurance with face and loan value, and 'Additional Information' including court proceedings, bankruptcies, repossessions, 'recent transfers of assets for less than full value', anticipated income increases, health, trusts, estates and retirement plans); V asset and liability analysis (cash, bank accounts, investments, insurance cash value, vehicles, real property, other assets, revolving credit, other liabilities, federal and state taxes owed, each with market value, liability, equity and monthly payment); VI monthly income and 'necessary living expenses' (wages for taxpayer and for spouse 'even if your spouse is not liable for the tax', interest, business income, rent, pensions; rent/house payment, groceries, allowable installment payments, utilities, transportation, insurance, medical, estimated tax payments, other) ending in 'Net Difference (income less necessary living expenses)'; VII certification 'Under penalties of perjury'.

value.keyOutput: Net Difference = monthly income less necessary living expenses

claim: Statute: the Secretary 'may enter into written agreements' for installment payment 'if the secretary determines that the agreement will facilitate collection'. An agreement 'shall remain in effect for the term of the agreement', except the Secretary may terminate it if information given before the agreement was 'inaccurate or incomplete' or collection is 'in jeopardy'; may alter, modify or terminate it if the taxpayer fails to pay an installment when due, fails to pay any other tax liability when due, or fails to provide a requested financial update; and may act on a significant change in financial condition only with notice 'no later than 30 days prior' stating the reasons. Prepayment is always allowed. The department's help pages, seen only in search snippets, say a plan requires filing and paying future returns timely, and that on default 'there is a possibility of liens, wage garnishment, bank attachments, citations, revocations of licenses, and further enforcement'. No cure or reinstatement procedure or fee is published.

claim: The down payment is up to the department, not fixed. The regulation (LAC 61:I.4919(B)(6)) reads: 'The taxpayer may be required to pay a down payment of 20 percent and to make installment payments by automatic bank draft.' The statute (R.S. 47:1576.2) says nothing about a down payment. The current form R-19026 (8/25) matches the rule: 'A down payment of 20 percent of the total amount due may be required for approval'. The previous form R-19026 (10/23) said it 'is required', and both versions' worksheet computes line 2 as 'Multiply Line 1 by 20 percent (.20)'. So it is exactly 20% when required, not 'up to 20%', and it is required at the secretary's discretion. The 2015 amnesty rule (LAC 61:I.4915) required 'no less than 20 percent', but that applied only to the 2014 amnesty program.
sourceDate: form R-19026 (8/25); regulation as amended LR 51:970 (July 2025); accessed 2026-10-11

The statute was read in Act 130 of 2015, enrolled HB 774 (https://www.legis.la.gov/Legis/ViewDocument.aspx?d=959823).

designImplication: Model the Louisiana down payment as 20% of the total due, required by default but able to be waived by the department, not as a sliding 0-20%. Because no criterion is published, the waiver is the department's call.

claim: The formal plan threshold is now $50,000, not $25,000. A September 2024 rule (LR 50:1293) changed LAC 61:I.4919(D): 'Informal installment agreements shall be allowed only if the amount owed is less than $50,000 and the payment period is 60 months or less. Formal installment agreements shall be required if the amount owed is $50,000 or more or the payment period exceeds 60 months. Information relative to the taxpayer's employment, bank account, credit, income statement, balance sheets, cash-flow data, and any other information shall be provided to the department upon request.' Before September 2024 the thresholds were $25,000 and 36 months. The rule's own preamble says it 'increases the maximum threshold and extends the payment period for informal installment agreements'. LDR's disclosure form for formal agreements is R-20223 (6/13), 'Statement of Financial Condition for Individuals, Formal Installment Agreement for Individuals'. It says it 'must include all household employment, assets, liabilities, income and expenses' and that 'Spouse and dependent information are required even though only one person is liable for the tax'. It covers personal information, prior returns and AGI, employment and garnishments in the last three years, dependants, and assets (cash, bank accounts, credit cards, securities, real property, vehicles, other assets).

value.disclosure: upon request: employment, bank account, credit, income statement, balance sheets, cash-flow data, other

uncertainty: The rule says disclosure is 'upon request', so a formal agreement does not automatically require the statement. R-20223 dates from 2013; whether LDR still uses it was not confirmed. Only its first two pages were read in full.
designImplication: Any premise that Louisiana's formal plan starts above $25,000 is out of date. Use $50,000 or more, or more than 60 months. A financial statement is a possible request, not a gate.

claim: R.S. 47:1576.2(A)(1): 'The secretary shall charge a fee of one hundred five dollars to establish a standard installment payment agreement'. (A)(3): 'the secretary shall not charge a fee to enter into a standard installment payment agreement with any taxpayer whose adjusted gross income is less than or equal to twenty-five thousand dollars.' The regulation repeats this and adds that the fee 'cannot be waived or applied against any tax debt'. Until July 2025 it also said the fee 'cannot be paid in installments'. A July 2025 rule (LR 51:970) deleted that clause, so the fee may now be paid within the installments. Form R-19026 (8/25) says the fee is waived 'if your Louisiana adjusted gross income reported on your most recently filed individual income tax return is less than or equal to $25,000' and that, if required, it 'must be submitted with your down payment'.

value.agiMeasure: Louisiana AGI on most recently filed individual return (per form)

The 8/25 form still tells taxpayers to send the fee with the down payment, which sits awkwardly with the 2025 rule. The fiscal note limits the installment option to informal agreements.

claim: An informal agreement may run up to 60 months (LAC 61:I.4919(D)(1), since September 2024). Above 60 months a formal agreement is required, and no maximum is published for it. The R-19026 (10/23) form said 'INSTALLMENT AGREEMENTS FOR INDIVIDUAL INCOME MUST BE A MINIMUM OF SIX (6) MONTHS'; the 8/25 form no longer says this. LDR's FAQ still describes 'a six-month installment payment plan' with 'monthly payments for one-sixth of the total balance due'.

claim: Regulation: 'If any installment payment is not paid on or before the dated fixed for its payment, the total outstanding balance shall be due and payable immediately upon notice and demand from secretary. All collection actions shall be reactivated.' 'Upon request of the taxpayer and the approval of the secretary, the installment agreement may be reinstated, provided the taxpayer pays the mandatory reinstatement fee in the amount of $60'. Form R-19026 (8/25): reinstatement costs '$60' or 'a new $105 installment fee if the agreement has been cancelled for 90 days or longer'; neither fee applies if Louisiana AGI is $25,000 or less. Failing to file returns or pay new taxes is also a default. An NSF debit adds an NSF fee and cancels the agreement. A state tax lien 'may be filed if the tax due is greater than $2,500 and/or if payments exceed 12 months'. Refund offsets continue during the plan. Penalty and interest keep accruing until paid in full.

claim: NMSA 7-1-21(C): 'At the time of entering into an installment agreement, the secretary shall require the affected taxpayer or person to furnish security for payment of the taxes admitted to be due according to the terms of the agreement, but if the taxpayer does not provide security, the secretary shall cause a notice of lien to be filed in accordance with the provisions of Section 7-1-38 NMSA 1978', which then is a lien on all the taxpayer's property in that county. TRD's practice divides plans in two: 'Short-term payment plans are those that have 12 or fewer installments ... Short-term payment plans do not require a lien to be filed.' 'Long-Term Agreements are formal, written agreements ... with installments from 13 to 72 months ... This type of agreement requires a lien or acceptable security to be filed.' Its self-service page: 'Plans longer than 12 months require that a lien be filed.'

claim: 7-1-21(A): 'No installment agreement shall prevent the accrual of interest otherwise provided by law.' TRD: interest accrues daily 'at the rate set for individual income tax purposes by the U.S. Internal Revenue Code (IRC)' and 'can change on a quarterly basis'. The rate is 7% a year (daily 0.019178082%) for July 1 - December 31, 2026, and was 6% for April 1 - June 30, 2026. 'Interest by law cannot be waived.' TRD also notes that 'interest and penalty continue to accrue' on a payment plan. The late payment penalty is 2% per month or part month, up to 20%.

claim: 7-1-21(A): 'Whenever justified by the circumstances, the secretary or the secretary's delegate may enter into a written agreement with a taxpayer in which the taxpayer admits conclusive liability for the entire amount of taxes due and agrees to make monthly installment payments ... but not for a period longer than seventy-two months.' An agreement 'is conclusive as to liability' but does not bar additional assessments (7-1-21(D)). Agreements over $1,000 are public records (7-1-21(F)); HB 198 (2025) would have raised this to $10,000, but it died in the Senate.

claim: The 100% penalty for three consecutive unfiled years is in ORS 305.992, not ORS 314.400(6). ORS 314.400(6) is a different 100% penalty, 'of any deficiency', for failing to file 'with intent to evade the tax' or filing a false return with that intent. ORS 305.992(1): 'If any returns required to be filed for state taxes ... are not filed for three consecutive years by the due date (including extensions) of the return required for the third consecutive year, there shall be a penalty for each year of 100 percent of the tax liability determined after credits and prepayments for each such year.' OAR 150-305-0480: the penalty 'may be imposed if: (a) The taxpayer was required to file returns for each tax year of three or more consecutive years ... and (b) All returns due during the three-year period are not filed by the due date (including extensions) of the return required for the third consecutive year.' A year with no filing requirement breaks the chain (Example 1). A return filed before the third year's due date, including a federal extension, keeps the penalty off (Example 9). No demand or notice is a condition; the trigger is the third due date passing. It applies to each year in the run with a net liability (tax after credits, withholding and prepayments), so a refund year carries none (Example 5). It can reach more than three years: Example 2 imposes it on 2013, 2014, 2015 and 2016. A department-prepared assessment under ORS 305.265(10) is not a 'return' that stops the clock. The department 'will not impose the 100 percent penalty ... for returns filed or a Notice of Assessment that have been assessed a lower failure-to-file penalty' (Examples 3 and 4).

value.base: net tax liability per year (tax less credits, withholding, prepayments)
value.trigger: no return for 3 consecutive required years by the 3rd year's due date incl. extensions
value.appliesTo: every year in the consecutive run with net liability

sourceDate: ORS 305.992 as amended 2025 c.371 s.7; OAR 150-305-0480 effective 2018-01-01; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: Official ORS text from the Oregon Legislature, and the official OAR from the Secretary of State (https://secure.sos.state.or.us/oard/view.action?ruleNumber=150-305-0480). ORS 314.400(6) was read in https://www.oregonlegislature.gov/bills_laws/ors/ors314.html.
uncertainty: The rule says 'may be imposed' while the statute says 'there shall be'; the rule's discretion is the 'lower penalty already assessed' carve-out under ORS 305.229.
designImplication: Correct the citation to ORS 305.992. Trigger it on the third consecutive required year passing its due date with none of the three filed, and apply 100% of net tax to every year in the run. Do not stack it on a year that already carries a lower failure-to-file assessment.

claim: ORS 305.992(2): 'The penalty imposed under this section is in addition to any other penalty imposed by law. However, the total amount of penalties imposed under the tax laws of this state for any tax year under this section, ORS 305.265 (13), 314.400, 323.403, 323.585 or 475C.722 may not exceed 100 percent of the tax liability.' The 314.400 penalties are: (1) 5% delinquency (late filing or late payment); (2)(a) 20% failure to file if more than three months late; and (2)(b) an extra 25% if no return follows a 30-day notice and demand and the department assesses. ORS 314.400(8) separately caps 314.400 plus 305.265(13) at 100% of the deficiency. So for a year caught by the three-year rule, 5% + 20% + 100% is cut back to a 100% total. OAR 150-305-0480 Example 3 shows a 50% failure-to-file penalty (5 + 20 + 25) on earlier years that is left at 50% and not raised to 100%.
sourceDate: ORS 305.992(2) as amended 2025 c.371 s.7; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: Official statute text for both 305.992 and 314.400.
uncertainty: The cap's base in 305.992(2) is 'tax liability' while 314.400(8)'s is 'deficiency'; for a non-filer these coincide, but the statute does not say which one governs if they differ.
designImplication: Compute 5% + 20% (+25% if assessed after demand) + 100%, then clamp the year's penalties to 100% of that year's tax. The three-year penalty adds at most 75 points over 5% and 20%.

claim: OAR 150-305-0068(3)(a)(E) lists 'The 100 percent penalty under ORS 305.992 for failure to file three consecutive reports or returns by the due date of the third year' as eligible for waiver. The 100% penalties under ORS 305.265(13) and 314.400(6) (intent to evade) are not eligible. A waiver needs a written request explaining the reason, filed before full payment or up to one year after it, and compliance with all filing requirements. Under (5) the department 'will waive all' of the penalty for circumstances beyond the taxpayer's control (death or serious illness, casualty, unavoidable absence, wrong written advice from the department or a professional); inability to pay does not count by itself. The one-time waiver under (6) does not cover the 305.992 penalty. Otherwise (8)(b), for non-payroll taxes, sets a schedule: 70% of the penalty is waived if the return is filed before any Request to File, Notice and Demand to File, or Combined Failure-to-File Notice; 50% if filed after such a notice; 25% if filed after a Notice of Determination and Assessment. Remaining after waiver: 30%, 50% or 75% of tax.

claim: G.L. c. 62C, s. 28, in full: 'If a person who has been notified by the commissioner that he has failed to file a return or has filed an incorrect or insufficient return refuses or neglects within thirty days after the date of such notification to file a proper return, or if a person has filed a false or fraudulent return or has filed a return with a willful attempt in any manner to defeat or evade the tax, the commissioner may determine the tax due, according to his best information and belief, and may assess the same at not more than double the amount so determined, which additional tax shall be in addition to the other penalties provided by this chapter.' Both verbs are 'may', so it is discretionary, with a ceiling of double and no floor. The regulation calls it a 'Double Deficiency Assessment' (830 CMR 62C.26.1(2), (13)), 'at up to double the amount of the tax due', and says it is 'a tax additional to any other remedies or penalties'. A non-filer may be assessed this way 'at any time', with no three-year limit.

value.nonFilerTrigger: no proper return within 30 days of the commissioner's notice

claim: DOR's published guidance (AP 633, 'Guidelines for the Waiver and Abatement of Penalties', dated 01/29/2025) describes when s.28 is NOT applied: 'If the taxpayer files a proper return within 30 days of the date of the Notice of Failure to File (NFF) or of the Notice of Incorrect or Insufficient Return (NIR), no § 28 penalty will be assessed.' The taxpayer may ask for more time before the 30 days run out. For fraud or willful evasion, the addition 'will be imposed, without notice'. Its examples show DOR assessing the full double after non-response to an NFF ('DOR assessed the taxpayers at double the amount of tax it determined was properly due'). No published DOR document gives a criterion for choosing a multiple below double, or for not using s.28 against a non-responder. The criteria published are for abatement afterwards (next entry), not for imposition.

claim: For a non-filer, notice is a precondition: the statute runs from 'notified by the commissioner that he has failed to file a return'. 830 CMR 62C.26.1(13)(c): 'The Commissioner will send the taxpayer a written notification, requesting that the taxpayer file a proper return'. It 'will ordinarily contain' the taxpayer's name, taxpayer ID, the type of tax, the period(s), 'An explanation of the double deficiency assessment that may be imposed if the taxpayer refuses to file a proper return', and other information. The assessment itself then needs a written notice of deficiency assessment under 830 CMR 62C.26.1(6)(f)-(i). DOR's form of the notification is the Notice of Failure to File (NFF), 'sent by mail' (AP 633). For a false or fraudulent return, no notice of intention to assess is required (830 CMR 62C.26.1(14)(b)).

claim: Abatable and appealable, with limits. Abatement is applied for under c. 62C, s. 37, within 3 years of filing the return, 2 years of assessment, or 1 year of payment, whichever is later. A refusal can be appealed to the Appellate Tax Board under s. 39. Section 38 bars abatement for anyone who has not filed the return for the period, and says that for a fraudulent return, or an incorrect or insufficient return not corrected after notice, 'the commissioner shall not abate the tax below double the amount for which the person assessed was properly taxable'. AP 633: 'Abatements of § 28 double assessments are governed by § 38'. Decisions are 'case-by-case' on 'reasonable cause which resulted in the failure to timely respond to an NFF or an NIR'. The same reasonable-cause criteria as the s.33 late-file and late-pay penalties apply, and a partial excuse can justify 'a pro-rata portion' of abatement. In AP 633's examples, a child's hospitalisation earned full abatement, while an unexplained non-response or 'the general press of other business' earned none. The Commissioner 'lacks the authority and has no discretion' to abate the s.28 amount for fraud or willful evasion.
